title: Biomanipulation as a Restoration Tool to Combat Eutrophication: Recent Advances and Future Challenges
authors: Jeppesen E, Søndergaard M, Lauridsen TL, Davidson TA, Liu Z, Mazzeo N, et al.
organism: Lake phytoplankton incl. cyanobacteria; planktivorous/benthivorous fish (roach, bream), piscivores, Daphnia
scale: Whole lakes, temperate and warm (e.g. 27 Danish shallow lakes with >200 kg fish/ha removed)
dose: Fish removal; figure shows target catch rising with lake TP (up to ~250 kg/ha/yr); single cases 213 t (226 kg/ha)
duration: Short-term (1-several years) vs long-term (decades) effects reviewed
result: Short-term effects of fish removal 'have often been successful, provided that they have been sufficiently strong', but long-term perspectives 'less positive'; repeated removals may be needed. External nutrient reduction remains the key measure; in-lake restoration only reinforces recovery.
env_effects: Changes the whole food web; clear-water lakes retain more P in sediment, raising internal loading if they revert to turbid; effects on biodiversity and lake metabolism discussed.

title: Lake Restoration by Fish Removal: Short- and Long-Term Effects in 36 Danish Lakes
authors: Søndergaard M, Liboriussen L, Pedersen AR, Jeppesen E
organism: Roach (Rutilus rutilus), bream (Abramis brama); phytoplankton incl. cyanobacteria
dose: 41-1360 kg fish/ha removed over 1-19 years (mostly within 2-4 years); 27 lakes >~200 kg/ha within 3 years (mean 410, range 190-706 kg/ha), 9 lakes <200 kg/ha (mean 91, range 41-160 kg/ha)
duration: Monitored up to ~10+ years after removal
result: In the 27 lakes with >200 kg/ha removed in 3 years, Chl a and suspended solids fell to 50-70% of pre-removal and Secchi depth nearly doubled over the first 8-10 years, with an effect in >75% of lakes; total algal biovolume fell 30-50% and cyanobacteria by >50% after 3-7 years (significant only in years 2-5). Chl a 'survival' was only ~10% after 5 years, and most variables drifted back toward pre-removal after ~10 years.
env_effects: Cryptophytes increased substantially (significant in years 3-4); submerged macrophytes increased; Secchi depth and SS changes were the most durable (mean survival >90% after 10 years). Lakes with <200 kg/ha removal showed no clear effects on nutrients or turbidity.
key_details: Before-after analysis of 36 mainly small, shallow, eutrophic Danish lakes (median 32 ha, median mean depth 1.8 m, pre-removal TP 0.061-0.437 mg/L) where planktivorous and benthivorous fish were removed; no untreated control lakes. Phytoplankton composition data came from only 10 lakes. Survival analysis showed Chl a and TP improvements were short-lived (mean survival ~10% after 5 years, wide confidence intervals), while Secchi depth and SS changes lasted longer. Long-term (>10-14 year) conclusions rest on 1-3 lakes. Pike fingerling stocking in some lakes was judged to have no significant effect.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record says Chl a, TP, TN and SS all fell to 50-70%; the paper gives 50-70% for Chl a and SS only (TP and TN 'substantial' but lower). Phytoplankton and cyanobacteria results are from 10 lakes, not 36, and Chl a gains were short-lived (~10% survival at 5 years) rather than lasting 6-10 years.

title: Repeated Fish Removal to Restore Lakes: Case Study of Lake Væng, Denmark—Two Biomanipulations during 30 Years of Monitoring
authors: Søndergaard M, Lauridsen TL, Johansson LS, Jeppesen E
organism: Roach and bream; phytoplankton; Elodea canadensis
dose: First removal 1986-1988: 4 tons fish (201,000 individuals; roach 98% by number, bream 62% by weight), ~50-70% of planktivorous/benthivorous biomass; second removal Oct 2007-May 2009: 2.8 tons
result: After each removal summer Chl a fell from 60-80 to 10-30 ug/L and Secchi rose from 0.6 m to 1.3-1.6 m (and >1.5 m after 2010), but the first clear-water state lasted only about a decade: Chl a climbed from 9.4 ug/L (1991) to 85 ug/L (2006) before the second removal.
env_effects: Macrophyte recovery; summer TP 0.12 -> 0.07 mg/L and TN 1.0 -> 0.4 mg/L; nutrient maxima shifted from summer to winter.
key_details: Whole-lake case study in shallow Lake Vaeng, Denmark (catchment 9 km2, retention 15-25 days, ~70% groundwater inflow), no control lake; 30 years of summer monitoring. Wastewater was diverted in 1981 but the lake stayed turbid (Chl a 76 ug/L in 1986). Fish removed with gill nets, traps, trawling and electrofishing. Clear periods 1989-1998 and 2009-2015 had significantly higher Secchi and lower Chl a than turbid years (t-tests, Bonferroni p<0.0025); summer TP 0.036-0.072 mg/L at high macrophyte cover vs 0.084-0.170 mg/L at low cover. After macrophytes returned, Chl a peaks shifted to winter/spring (up to 96 ug/L).
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's framing is correct; add that the first biomanipulation's benefit decayed after ~10 years (return to turbid 1999-2008), which is why a second removal was needed.

title: Freshwater food web biomanipulation: A powerful tool for water quality improvement, but maintenance is required
organism: Planktivorous and piscivorous fish, zooplankton, algae
scale: Deep stratified lakes vs shallow lakes/ponds; six manipulation categories
dose: Planktivore additions, complete planktivore removals, piscivore additions
result: Planktivore removals in deep lakes often reduce algae at first, but ungrazable algae take over and biomass returns to pre-manipulation levels; shallow-lake removals are more stable. Piscivore additions to deep lakes 'seldom result in more than short periods of algal control'. The consensus is that 'maintenance is required'.
env_effects: Restructures food webs; species substitutions (invertebrate predators, macrophytes, ungrazable algae); reinvasion by planktivores.

title: Possibilities and Limits for Controlling Eutrophication by Biomanipulation
organism: Piscivorous and zooplanktivorous fish, Daphnia, phytoplankton
scale: Long-term whole-lake experiments: Bautzen reservoir and Lake Gräfenhain
dose: Strong to extremely strong enhancement of piscivorous fish stock
result: Top-down effects were strong at the top of the food web, but at the phytoplankton level only composition changed and 'mean biomass is not reduced'. Sustained reduction of phytoplankton biomass is expected only below a P-loading threshold.
env_effects: Hard to control 0+ fish of the stocked piscivores; invertebrate predators can compensate for fish predation.

title: Do high concentrations of microcystin prevent Daphnia control of phytoplankton?
authors: Chislock MF, Sarnelle O, Jernigan LM, Wilson AE
organism: Daphnia pulicaria vs toxic Microcystis and Anabaena
scale: Exp. 1: 4200 L enclosures in MSU Lake 2, Michigan (2 Daphnia vs 4 control enclosures after two Daphnia enclosures were invaded by fish); Exp. 2: 160 L enclosures in two hypereutrophic Auburn, Alabama catfish ponds (F19, F20), 2 Daphnia vs 2 control per pond
dose: Daphnia pulicaria stocked at ~0.3 animals/L (Exp. 1) or ~0.15 animals/L as an equal mix of three clones (Exp. 2); all four clones came from southern Michigan lakes; Exp. 2 enclosures fertilized biweekly with N and P
duration: Exp. 1: 2 July-6 August 2007 (~5 weeks); Exp. 2: 22 September-24 November 2010 (~50 days after stocking)
result: In Michigan (initial Chl a 130 µg/L, microcystin >3 rising to ~6 µg/L), Daphnia cut total phytoplankton 74% vs controls by week 3 (P = 0.010), and Microcystis 4-fold, Oscillatoria 56-fold, Anabaena 20-fold by day 28. In Alabama (microcystin 40 and 180 µg/L), mean effect sizes were 4.5 and 7.4 (about 78% and 86% less phytoplankton) and Microcystis fell 3.8- and 19.6-fold, but cyanobacteria still dominated all enclosures.
env_effects: Daphnia marginally reduced microcystin in Michigan (P = 0.063) and significantly reduced it in both Alabama ponds; microcystin rose in the Michigan enclosures overall. Community stayed cyanobacteria-dominated (no shift in relative composition).
key_details: Two enclosure experiments testing whether very high microcystin prevents Daphnia pulicaria grazing control. Replication was low: Exp. 1 had only 2 Daphnia enclosures (fish invaded two others), Exp. 2 had 2 per treatment per pond. Daphnia grew exponentially (r = 0.24/day) despite microcystin and reduced absolute biomass of all cyanobacteria, but relative dominance by cyanobacteria (Microcystis) was unchanged. Microcystis colonies were of edible size (ESD 28 and 70 µm). The Alabama experiment was in autumn and fertilized to maintain the bloom.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record says 'mixture of three cyanobacteria-adapted clones (Alabama)'; the clones came from Michigan lakes and were stocked into Alabama ponds. Record implies Daphnia raised microcystin; it rose in the Michigan enclosures but Daphnia marginally lowered it vs controls and significantly lowered it in Alabama. Only 2 Daphnia enclosures in Exp. 1.

title: Controlling Harmful Cyanobacteria: Taxa-Specific Responses of Cyanobacteria to Grazing by Large-Bodied Daphnia in a Biomanipulation Scenario
authors: Urrutia-Cordero P, Ekvall MK, Hansson L-A
organism: Daphnia magna vs natural cyanobacteria (Aphanizomenon, Dolichospermum, Microcystis, Planktothrix)
scale: Six 10 L containers (9 L filtered lake water) incubated in eutrophic Lake Ringsjön, Sweden (40 km2), plus 19-yr lake monitoring
duration: 3-day incubations, three times in one summer; monitoring 1996-2014 (biomanipulation since 2005)
result: Daphnia grazing reduced total cyanobacteria and phytoplankton and suppressed about 66% of tested bloom-forming taxa, but Dolichospermum crassum grew faster under grazing when it dominated. Lake fish reduction raised Daphnia abundance 50% and body size 20%.
env_effects: Taxa-specific: grazing can favour ungrazed filamentous cyanobacteria; authors say grazer control alone may not be sufficient and nutrient reduction is preferable.

title: Short-term fish predation destroys resilience of zooplankton communities and prevents recovery of phytoplankton control by zooplankton grazing
authors: Ersoy Z, Brucet S, Bartrons M, Mehner T
organism: Juvenile perch (Perca fluviatilis), lake zooplankton and phytoplankton
scale: 10 enclosures (~1000 L; 6 with fish, 4 without) with natural lake plankton
dose: ~20 g wet mass/m3 juvenile perch for 4 days, then removed by electrofishing
result: Four days of fish predation removed large zooplankton (calanoids) permanently; total zooplankton biomass recovered and even exceeded pre-fish levels, but small cladocerans and rotifers dominated and phytoplankton escaped grazer control. Only fish-free enclosures kept phytoplankton controlled.
env_effects: Shows fragility of grazer control: brief planktivore pulses (e.g. young-of-year fish) can undo biomanipulation.

title: Nontraditional biomanipulation: A powerful ecotechnology to combat cyanobacterial blooms in eutrophic freshwaters
authors: Chen J, Liu J, Han S, Su H, Xia W, Wang H, et al. (Xie P)
organism: Silver and bighead carp vs Microcystis and other cyanobacteria
scale: 42 experiments reviewed plus a whole-lake case (Lake Donghu, China)
dose: Silver and bighead carp stocking; enclosure trials used roughly 8-480 g/m3; in Lake Donghu the 2022 release was doubled vs 2021 (silver:bighead 2:1), raising standing stock to 82 g/m3 (March 2022) and 192 g/m3 (September 2022)
result: Filter-feeding carp substantially reduced cyanobacteria in 88% of 42 experiments; in Lake Donghu Microcystis bloom coverage fell from 87% (2021) to 0% (2022). Carp graze colonial Microcystis better than filamentous forms.
env_effects: Several enclosure and pond studies were negative (e.g. Villerest Reservoir: cyanobacteria increased at 8-32 g/m3 silver carp; bighead carp in Polish ponds raised filamentous Anabaena 4-fold to 70-fold). Carp handle colonial Microcystis better than filamentous cyanobacteria; in Donghu TN, TP and NH4+ fell (1.04 to 0.75, 0.13 to 0.10, 0.15 to 0.12 mg/L) despite over 4x more fish.
key_details: Review by the Lake Donghu (Institute of Hydrobiology) group of 42 enclosure, pond and whole-lake experiments; 88% showed substantial cyanobacteria reductions by filter-feeding carp. Most enclosure trials had only 2-3 replicates per treatment in small enclosures (e.g. 6-100 m2); examples include 91% reduction of M. aeruginosa in Dongzhou Reservoir enclosures and 60-93% Microcystis reduction within 3-7 days in an Indian lake. The Donghu whole-lake case is a single before/after comparison (bloom in 2021 after fish stock declined since 2004; no bloom in 2022 after doubling the fish release and limiting fishing to winter) with no control lake. Authors also report commercial fishing profit from the stock.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record does not mention that the review itself lists negative trials (fish raising cyanobacteria, especially filamentous forms and at low stocking), or that the Donghu result is an uncontrolled one-year before/after comparison by the proponents' own group.

title: Role of Microcystins in Poisoning and Food Ingestion Inhibition of Daphnia galeata Caused by the Cyanobacterium Microcystis aeruginosa
authors: Rohrlack T, Dittmann E, Henning M, Börner T, Kohl J-G
organism: Daphnia galeata vs Microcystis aeruginosa PCC7806 (wild type and mcy- mutant)
dose: M. aeruginosa PCC7806 wild type vs mcy- knockout mutant at 20 mm3/L biovolume (reference strain HUB 5-3 for ingestion); 14C-labelled cells for ingestion
duration: Ingestion assays (repeated 7-9 times); 5-day life-table survival tests (4 replicates) at 20 C
result: Wild-type PCC7806 killed D. galeata with a time to 50% mortality of 1.2-2.0 days, while no animals died on the microcystin-free mutant. Both variants were ingested at the same low rate, 75% below the harmless reference strain HUB 5-3.
env_effects: Grazer mortality and feeding inhibition by toxic cyanobacteria.
key_details: Lab test separating toxicity from feeding inhibition using a microcystin-synthetase knockout of the same strain. Ingestion measured by 14C-labelled cells (n = 7 for PCC7806 variants, n = 9 for HUB 5-3). Survival compared against a no-food control in four repeat experiments; wild type differed from starvation (log rank P < 0.001) and mutant animals survived better than starved controls (P < 0.025). Daphnia on wild type became inactive after about 5 h. Single strain and single Daphnia clone.
fulltext_discrepancy: None material; adds the LT50 of 1.2-2.0 days and the 75% ingestion reduction.

title: Control of the harmful alga Cochlodinium polykrikoides by the naked ciliate Strombidinopsis jeokjo in mesocosm enclosures
authors: Jeong HJ, Kim JS, Yoo YD, Kim ST, Song JY, Kim TH, et al.
organism: Ciliate Strombidinopsis jeokjo vs Cochlodinium (Margalefidinium) polykrikoides
scale: ~60 L in-situ mesocosms with natural red-tide water (Korea)
result: Per search-result summary, S. jeokjo 'eliminated most C. polykrikoides cells in a short period' and grew well in the mesocosms; the authors suggest large-scale cultures could control red tides in small areas. Exact numbers not seen.
env_effects: Introduction changed total diatom and heterotrophic dinoflagellate concentrations vs controls.

title: The ability of the branchiopod, Artemia salina, to graze upon harmful algal blooms caused by Alexandrium fundyense, Aureococcus anophagefferens, and Cochlodinium polykrikoides
authors: Marcoval MA, Pan J, Tang YZ, Gobler CJ
organism: Artemia salina (non-native) and Acartia tonsa (native copepod) vs Alexandrium fundyense, Aureococcus anophagefferens, Cochlodinium polykrikoides
scale: 50 mL flasks (n=5) with cultures, plus field bottle incubations of natural blooms from Long Island, NY estuaries
dose: 0.24 Artemia salina nauplii/mL (vs 0.48 Acartia tonsa copepodites/mL); culture HAB densities e.g. A. fundyense 290-1500 cells/mL
duration: 24 h grazing/mortality incubations (48 h for C. polykrikoides field tests)
result: In natural bloom water, Artemia nauplii cut C. polykrikoides by an average 57 +/- 19% (max 78%) in 48 h, A. fundyense by 48 +/- 9%, and A. anophagefferens by 24-73% in five of six experiments. Artemia mortality was 47 +/- 2.4% in A. fundyense blooms versus 13-18% in the other blooms.
env_effects: Artemia is non-native to NY estuaries (introduction risk); grazers suffer high mortality on toxic Alexandrium.
key_details: Lab grazing experiments compared the non-native brine shrimp Artemia salina with the native copepod Acartia tonsa on cultured A. anophagefferens (2 strains), C. polykrikoides and A. fundyense, with Rhodomonas salina as the non-harmful control diet (n=5 flasks per treatment). Artemia clearance rates on C. polykrikoides (450-500 ul/ind/h) were the highest of any alga tested; Acartia did not feed on A. fundyense at all. Mortality on A. fundyense was 43% (Artemia) and 72% (Acartia), significantly above other diets. Field bottle tests with bloom water compared nauplii additions to no-grazer controls; reductions were smaller at high cell densities (31-35% above 1600 C. polykrikoides cells/mL). Artemia is non-native, and field-scale release was not tested.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's '25 field experiments... six New York estuaries' was not verified in the text read; field results give mean reductions of 57% (C. polykrikoides), 48% (A. fundyense) and 24-73% (A. anophagefferens), so effect_pct can be filled.
